zh.q: 同一支铁钉，凭什么既能生锈、又能做暖贴、还能被保护？
zh.concl: 这四样东西是同一个原理的四种用法：铁在潮湿空气里的腐蚀是电化学腐蚀，钢铁腐蚀主要是吸氧腐蚀（教材原话）。
points: ① 和 ② 只差一样：管里的溶液是食盐水还是稀盐酸。
④ 里被保护的铁片「作为正极（阴极）」不被腐蚀，保护它的是更活泼的锌。
暖贴不是「发热剂」，是让铁按可控速率腐蚀、把化学能变成热。

zh.q: 导管里的水凭什么自己往上爬？
zh.concl: 钢铁的吸氧腐蚀要「溶有一定量的氧气」：管内 O₂ 在碳表面得电子被消耗，气体体积变小，水柱被大气压顶上去。
points: 水柱上升不是「铁在吸水」，是管内氧气被消耗、压强变小。
隔氧就完全不升——这是判断「是不是吸氧腐蚀」最直接的办法。
铁锈（Fe₂O₃·xH₂O）疏松地盖在表面，挡不住继续腐蚀。

zh.q: 铁钉是纯铁，管里哪来的「正极」？
zh.concl: 不纯的金属与电解质溶液接触才发生原电池反应：钢铁里「铁和少量单质碳」构成原电池，碳作正极、铁作负极被氧化（教材原话）。
points: 碳粉是阴极：它不消耗，只提供 O₂ 得电子的地方，所以碳越多腐蚀越快。
纯铁没有碳、没有微电池，所以比生铁耐腐蚀。
这条也解释了暖贴为什么一定要配碳粉（第 6 步）。

zh.q: 把食盐水换成稀盐酸，同样的装置怎么反过来了？
zh.concl: 在酸性环境中，腐蚀过程中不断有 H₂ 放出，所以叫析氢腐蚀：负极 Fe − 2e⁻ = Fe²⁺，正极 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ = H₂↑（教材原话）。
points: 两种腐蚀的负极完全相同（都是 Fe − 2e⁻ = Fe²⁺），只有正极不同。
所以「检验 Fe²⁺」分不出类型，能分的是「有没有气泡 / 水柱升不升」。
钢铁在潮湿空气里以吸氧腐蚀为主，因为水膜的酸性通常很弱或呈中性。

zh.q: 铁里流走的电子，最后去了哪里？
zh.concl: 铁和少量单质碳构成原电池，铁作负极被氧化，氧气（或 H⁺）在碳表面得电子被还原（教材原话）。
points: 电子走在铁内部（不是水膜里），从铁表面流到碳粒。
O₂ 是在碳表面得电子，不是在铁表面——所以碳多的地方腐蚀快。
中性时生成 OH⁻（水膜变碱），酸性时生成 H₂ 跑掉，这一条决定水柱往哪边动。

zh.q: 同一件事，凭什么暖贴能发热而我们感觉不到铁钉发热？
zh.concl: 市售暖贴是利用金属的电化学腐蚀原理制作的：铁粉按可控速率被氧化，化学能变成热，发热温和、放热时间长（教材原话）。
points: 暖贴的「热」来自铁的氧化，和液柱上升是同一个反应的两种表现。
配比决定的是速率（升温快慢），不是最高温度。
用它在任何场合都要留一条透气路——第 7 步就讲捂住会怎样。

zh.q: 把暖贴塞进密封袋，它还热得起来吗？
zh.concl: 吸氧腐蚀必须以氧气为原料：没有 O₂，正极的 2H₂O + O₂ + 4e⁻ = 4OH⁻ 就无从发生，铁粉、碳粉、食盐水配得再好也不发热。
points: 错误操作链①：把暖贴捂住 / 装进密封袋 → 隔绝 O₂ → 正极反应停 → 放热为零，温度回落到室温（偏差 −28.5 ℃）。
错误操作链②：食盐水换成蒸馏水 → 离子太少 → 30 min 液柱只有 10 mm（偏差 −48 mm）。
错误操作链③：不加碳粉 → 只有铁钉当电极 → 30 min 只有 23 mm（偏差 −35 mm）。

zh.q: 同一支铁钉，接上一块锌，凭什么就不生锈了？
zh.concl: 镁、锌比铁活泼，它们成为原电池的负极、不断遭受腐蚀（需要定期检查、更换），而作为正极的钢铁设备就被保护起来（教材原话）。
points: 液柱上升 ≠ 铁在生锈：管内氧气被谁消耗都一样会让水柱升，判断铁有没有被腐蚀只能看 Fe²⁺ 检验。
牺牲阳极法让被保护的金属当阴极（正极），它自己不再失电子。
锌要定期检查更换——它是在「替」铁被腐蚀。

zh.q: 考核：设计一只 45 ℃ 以上、能稳住 15 秒的暖贴
zh.concl: 考核没有新结论：把「铁粉 + 碳粉 + 食盐水 + 透气」同时照顾好，暖贴才又热又稳；同一套原理反过来用，就是第 8 步的防护。
points: 碳粉要够（≥ 20 %）：不够升温慢，10 min 只有 31.8 ℃。
必须透气：捂住就完全不发热（20.0 ℃）。
时间也要够：参考配比下 20 min 才到 48.2 ℃。

en.q: How can the same iron nail rust, make a hand warmer, and also be protected?
en.concl: These four things are four uses of one principle: iron corroding in moist air is electrochemical corrosion, and steel corrodes mainly by oxygen absorption (textbook wording).
points: ① and ② differ in just one thing: the solution in the tube is salt water or dilute hydrochloric acid.
In ④ the protected iron sheet acts as the positive electrode (cathode) and doesn't corrode; it is protected by the more active zinc.
A hand warmer isn't a "heating agent"; it lets iron corrode at a controlled rate, turning chemical energy into heat.

en.q: Why does the water in the delivery tube climb on its own?
en.concl: Oxygen-absorption corrosion of steel needs "a certain amount of dissolved oxygen": O₂ in the tube gains electrons at the carbon surface and is consumed, the gas volume shrinks, and atmospheric pressure pushes the water up.
points: The water column rising isn't "iron absorbing water"; oxygen in the tube is used up and the pressure drops.
With oxygen excluded it doesn't rise at all; this is the most direct way to tell whether it's oxygen-absorption corrosion.
Rust (Fe₂O₃·xH₂O) covers the surface loosely and doesn't stop further corrosion.

en.q: The nail is pure iron, so where does the "positive electrode" in the tube come from?
en.concl: Impure metals in contact with electrolyte solutions undergo galvanic reactions: in steel, "iron and a little elemental carbon" form a galvanic cell, with carbon as the positive electrode and iron as the negative electrode, which is oxidized (textbook wording).
points: Carbon powder is the cathode: it isn't consumed, it just provides a place for O₂ to gain electrons, so more carbon means faster corrosion.
Pure iron has no carbon and no micro-cells, so it resists corrosion better than pig iron.
This also explains why a hand warmer must contain carbon powder (step 6).

en.q: Replace the salt water with dilute hydrochloric acid: why does the same setup reverse?
en.concl: In an acidic environment H₂ is continuously released during corrosion, hence the name hydrogen-evolution corrosion: negative electrode Fe − 2e⁻ = Fe²⁺, positive electrode 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ = H₂↑ (textbook wording).
points: The negative electrode is exactly the same in both kinds of corrosion (Fe − 2e⁻ = Fe²⁺); only the positive electrode differs.
So "testing for Fe²⁺" can't tell the types apart; what can is "are there bubbles / does the column rise".
Steel in moist air corrodes mainly by oxygen absorption, because the water film is usually only weakly acidic or neutral.

en.q: Where do the electrons leaving the iron finally go?
en.concl: Iron and a little elemental carbon form a galvanic cell; iron, the negative electrode, is oxidized, and oxygen (or H⁺) gains electrons at the carbon surface and is reduced (textbook wording).
points: Electrons travel through the iron (not the water film), flowing from the iron surface to the carbon grain.
O₂ gains electrons at the carbon surface, not the iron surface, so corrosion is faster where there is more carbon.
In neutral conditions OH⁻ forms (the water film turns basic); in acid H₂ forms and escapes; this decides which way the water column moves.

en.q: It's the same process, so why does a hand warmer get hot when we can't feel a nail heating up?
en.concl: Commercial hand warmers are made using the electrochemical corrosion of metal: iron powder is oxidized at a controlled rate, turning chemical energy into heat that is gentle and long-lasting (textbook wording).
points: The heat of a hand warmer comes from oxidation of iron; it and the rising water column are two signs of the same reaction.
The mix ratio sets the rate (how fast it warms up), not the maximum temperature.
Wherever it's used it needs an air path; step 7 shows what happens if it's covered.

en.q: Put a hand warmer in a sealed bag: can it still get warm?
en.concl: Oxygen-absorption corrosion requires oxygen as a reactant: without O₂ the positive-electrode reaction 2H₂O + O₂ + 4e⁻ = 4OH⁻ can't happen, and no matter how well the iron powder, carbon powder and salt water are mixed, there's no heat.
points: Wrong-action chain ①: cover the hand warmer / put it in a sealed bag → O₂ cut off → positive-electrode reaction stops → zero heat, temperature falls to room temperature (deviation −28.5 ℃).
Wrong-action chain ②: replace salt water with distilled water → too few ions → only 10 mm of column in 30 min (deviation −48 mm).
Wrong-action chain ③: no carbon powder → only the nail as electrode → only 23 mm in 30 min (deviation −35 mm).

en.q: Attach a piece of zinc to the same iron nail: why does it stop rusting?
en.concl: Magnesium and zinc are more active than iron; they become the negative electrode of the galvanic cell and keep corroding (and must be checked and replaced regularly), while the steel equipment, as the positive electrode, is protected (textbook wording).
points: A rising column ≠ iron rusting: whoever consumes the oxygen in the tube, the column rises; whether the iron is corroding can only be judged by the Fe²⁺ test.
The sacrificial-anode method makes the protected metal the cathode (positive electrode), so it no longer loses electrons itself.
The zinc must be checked and replaced regularly; it is corroding "in place of" the iron.

en.q: Assessment: design a hand warmer above 45 ℃ that holds steady for 15 seconds
en.concl: The assessment has no new conclusion: only by taking care of "iron powder + carbon powder + salt water + air" together is the hand warmer both warm and steady; the same principle used in reverse is the protection of step 8.
points: Enough carbon is needed (≥ 20 %): too little and it warms slowly, only 31.8 ℃ at 10 min.
It must breathe: covered, it produces no heat at all (20.0 ℃).
It also needs time: with the reference mix it only reaches 48.2 ℃ at 20 min.
